ideas.title: Your Celebrity Feed Arrives on Cardboard
ideas.era: Britain, 1860s; Camille Silvy photograph of Adelina Patti identified as 1865
ideas.premise: What if today following your favorite performer meant collecting a small mounted photographic card instead of refreshing a feed?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Celebrity Feed Arrives on Cardboard history

rationale.curiosity: The physical feed reveal is grounded in a particular theatrical portrait rather than a generic nostalgia claim.
rationale.cast_comedy: Rex can invent a fictional subscription scheme while Mia separates a collectible portrait from actual celebrity access.
rationale.modern_contrast: Collecting and displaying performer photographs creates an immediate contrast with online following.
rationale.primary_sources: Victoria and Albert Museum identifies a Silvy portrait of Adelina Patti and explains the card format; sales totals and individual behavior remain unknown.

cast_gags.crow: Raven introduces a real portrait format and labels the modern feed analogy as a joke.
cast_gags.pip: Pip looks for an imaginary refresh button on a mounted paper portrait.
cast_gags.mia: Mia explains that collecting a photograph is not a personal message from the performer.
cast_gags.rex: Rex offers a fictional premium cardboard-feed membership with a larger empty album.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy turns the album page and asks whether that counts as an update.

sources.institution: Victoria and Albert Museum via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Guy Little Theatrical Photograph; Camille Silvy; Adelina Patti as Linda, 1865; catalog range 1860/1869; Guy Little bequest
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The artifact and curatorial account support a small theatrical photograph and collecting context. The feed, refresh button and membership are fiction. A portrait in a role is not a photograph of an actual event in that role; no invented signature, personal endorsement, sales figure, or universal collecting practice.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Establish the exact inventory number and distinguish the portrait's 1865 identification from the broader catalog decade before expanding the distribution or pricing story.

ideas.title: Your Beach Changing Room Needs a Parking Space
ideas.era: Britain; 1788 artwork and separate 1901 Great Yarmouth photographic context
ideas.premise: What if today a trip to the beach required a changing room on wheels that went towards the water with you, like a historical bathing machine?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Beach Changing Room Needs a Parking Space history

rationale.curiosity: An unexpectedly mobile room creates a specific visual reveal rather than a vague Victorian anecdote.
rationale.cast_comedy: A fictional parking dispute can escalate from Pip wanting a swim to Rex managing an entire wheeled room.
rationale.modern_contrast: Current beach convenience contrasts with a documented historical contraption.
rationale.primary_sources: A dated Yale artwork and a museum archive explanation are identified; neither establishes a universal legal requirement.

cast_gags.crow: Raven opens a fictional travel review about bringing the room to the beach.
cast_gags.pip: Pip packs a towel and discovers the fictional booking also includes a wheeled cabin.
cast_gags.mia: Mia points out the difference between the documented object and Rex's invented parking policy.
cast_gags.rex: Rex issues a tiny imaginary parking permit for an enormous changing room.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy carries a miniature reserved sign to the empty stretch of beach.

ideas.title: The Productivity Upgrade Is an Iron Blade
ideas.era: Roman Britain; object catalog date 1-399 CE; Great Witcombe findspot
ideas.premise: What if today the productivity consultant offered Pip a Roman plough coulter instead of another farm dashboard, because the heavy soil needed a physical cut?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Productivity Upgrade Is an Iron Blade history

rationale.curiosity: A physical mechanism supplies a useful payoff, although the hook is less surprising than the other candidates.
rationale.cast_comedy: The joke targets Rex's abstract promises while Mia explains the actual order of operations.
rationale.modern_contrast: An imaginary software-sales pitch contrasts with a documented soil-working tool.
rationale.primary_sources: British Museum identifies coulter 1819,0313.1 and describes its action ahead of the plough-share; no numerical yield evidence is supplied.

cast_gags.crow: Raven distinguishes a genuine mechanism from a fictional consultant's grand promises.
cast_gags.pip: Pip shows a harmless cutaway of difficult soil instead of another chart.
cast_gags.mia: Mia uses an editorial diagram to show the vertical cut before the share undercuts the furrow.
cast_gags.rex: Rex tries to invoice the imaginary dashboard before noticing it cannot cut anything.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy labels the harmless model with two removable editorial arrows, keeping all real blades off the set.

ideas.title: Your Pocket Map Has No Location Dot
ideas.era: Britain; John Bleuler globe dated 1824 in Science Museum interpretation
ideas.premise: What if today your pocket travel display was a miniature terrestrial globe with constellations inside its case, with no location dot to tell you where you were?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Pocket Map Has No Location Dot history

rationale.curiosity: The reveal turns an assumed digital feature into a concrete missing capability on a real historical object type.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip can attempt to use an educational object for navigation while Mia corrects Rex's fictional product pitch.
rationale.modern_contrast: Pocket information before a smartphone provides a visual comparison without claiming equivalent functions.
rationale.primary_sources: Science Museum interpretation identifies Bleuler and 1824, but no standalone accession record or primary manual has been inspected.

cast_gags.crow: Raven opens the world in miniature without pretending it was a GPS.
cast_gags.pip: Pip turns the globe searching for an imaginary you-are-here dot.
cast_gags.mia: Mia opens the case to reveal the documented constellation display.
cast_gags.rex: Rex claims a fictional premium offline-navigation tier, then asks Mia which way is north.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy puts a removable modern prop sticker on the desk map rather than altering the historical globe.
